claims.text: High-temperature XRD can be integrated with real-time thermogravimetric monitoring under a controlled oxidizing atmosphere.
The integrated method can simultaneously capture oxidation kinetics and transient phase transformations.
The integrated method measures oxidation through weight gain and oxide-scale growth.
Integrated in situ measurements are more accurate than separate ex situ measurements.
Synchrotron radiation improves the time resolution and sensitivity of high-temperature XRD.
Temperatures of 750–1100 °C are suitable for studying high-temperature phase stability in the proposed class of alloys.
Oxidation and phase evolution occur concurrently under the proposed high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Oxide scales dynamically form and evolve on the alloy surface during high-temperature oxidation.
Oxide-scale evolution coincides with phase transformations in the underlying bulk alloy.
High-temperature alloys can undergo temperature-dependent phase transformations or decomposition.
Continuous TGA weight gain records the kinetics of oxidation.
Real-time XRD detects the emergence or transformation of crystalline phases.
Simultaneously acquired XRD and TGA data permit temporal correlation of oxidation kinetics with phase transformations.
Ex situ methods can miss transient phase behavior.
The integrated method will reveal synchronous changes in sample weight and phase state.
The integrated method will provide a more detailed and temporally correlated understanding than separate TGA and post-mortem XRD.
Post-mortem XRD provides only discontinuous snapshots of phase evolution.
The method's advantages are limited to high-temperature, precisely controlled oxidizing atmospheres.
At lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing environments, coupling between oxidation and phase transformation is less pronounced.
Very rapid phase transitions and overlapping signals in complex systems may limit the method's time resolution and interpretability.
